title: The Danza Criolla: Villoldo, El Choclo, and the Tune That Left Buenos Aires Without Him
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Barracas, the birth on the south side
stops.date_confidence: attested: es. and en.wikipedia agree on 16 February 1861 and on Barracas. The birth name Ghigiola Roggio and the parents come from es.wikipedia alone, which spells the surname both Ghigiola and Ghigiolla; no civil register was consulted. Coordinate is the OSM Barracas centroid, adopted to reconcile two research lenses that pinned the barrio 1.2 km apart.
stops.campa: On the south side of Buenos Aires, in Barracas, where the saladeros salt hides by the Riachuelo and the warehouses stand with their backs to the river, a son is born to Juan Ghigiola and Victoria Roggio and is registered Angel Gregorio. The city above him is filling with Italians and Spaniards off the boats; the barrio around him has been left behind by the rich families who fled the fever north. He will take the name Villoldo, five pen names besides, and give this river-mouth city its first songs about itself.
suggested_refs: The parish and civil registers of Barracas for February 1861, not consulted in this research pass

stops.name: Barracas, the barrio the fever emptied
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the barrio history is documented (es.wikipedia, 'Barracas'), but no source ties a street, a house, a school, or his parents' occupations to Villoldo. The 1871 date marks the yellow fever epidemic, not an event in his life.
stops.campa: Barracas belonged to the Rosas years and to money; the yellow fever drives the wealthy north to Belgrano and Palermo and leaves the southern barrios to the conventillos, the tanneries, and the dockmen. The boy grows up in that emptied grandeur, among tenement patios where Genoese, Andalusian, and criollo speech grind against each other into lunfardo. No street, no house, no school is recorded for him. What the barrio taught him surfaces later, in the mouths of the characters he writes and in the slang he puts on paper first.
suggested_refs: The conventillos of Barracas and Constitución in the decades after the 1871 epidemic

stops.name: La Boca, the Riachuelo docks and the academias de baile
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: no source places Villoldo at any named address in La Boca. This stop records the documented milieu of tango's formation, not a proven visit. The pin merges a duplicate 'Puerto de Buenos Aires' stop that carried the same waterfront coordinate; the immigrant port proper is in Retiro.
stops.campa: Along the Riachuelo the Italian dockworkers unload coal and hides, and behind the wharves stand the bars, the brothels, and the academias de baile where men pay women to dance with them. Historians of tango point here and to the southern barrios for the music's formation: habanera, milonga, candombe drum, and the accordion of the port. No document places Villoldo on these docks. He grows up on the same river a mile upstream, and the slang his lyrics are written in is the slang spoken here, on this water, by these men.
suggested_refs: The academias de baile and dockside bars of La Boca and Barracas in the 1880s
sources: General tango historiography on La Boca's role in tango's origins; no Villoldo-specific citation located

stops.name: Buenos Aires, four trades before the guitar
stops.date_confidence: attested for the trades themselves (en.wikipedia lists typographer, tram driver, circus clown, journalist, and self-taught musicianship); reconstruction for everything else. No employer, address, or ordering of years is given by any source, and 1885 is a placeholder inside the run of years, not a documented date. The pin is the corpus's canonical Buenos Aires coordinate.
stops.campa: Before music feeds him he sets type in a printing house, drives a tram through the centre, paints his face as a clown in a circus ring, and writes for newspapers. No employer, address, or order of years survives for any of the four. He teaches himself guitar and singing without a master. Each trade leaves him something. Type shows him how a verse looks set in lead. The ring teaches timing. The newspapers pay him to write about the city for the people living in it, and the tram carries him through every barrio of it in a working day.
suggested_refs: The Buenos Aires printing trade and tramway companies of the 1880s, in which no employer of Villoldo has been identified

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the criollo songs collected
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by en.wikipedia, which names a compilation of criollo folk songs published in 1889; no publisher, title page, or surviving copy was located, and the month and day default to January 1. Pin is the canonical Buenos Aires coordinate.
stops.campa: He publishes a compilation of criollo songs, the payador repertoire of the countryside gathered by a man of the port city. The gauchos are being fenced out of the pampa as he prints them; the criollo verse forms, the decimas and payadas traded between singers, are moving into the cafes of Buenos Aires along with the men displaced. Villoldo collects them, then begins to write them himself, in the voice of a townsman who claims the criollo name for the paved streets.
stops.quote: Aquí tienen el criollo más criollo,
stops.quote_source: 'El Criollo Más Criollo,' opening line, lyrics as printed on Letras.com, credited there to Ángel Villoldo
suggested_refs: The 1889 compilation of criollo songs, no copy of which was located in this research pass
sources: Letras.com, artist index for Ángel Villoldo

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the harmonica-and-guitar apparatus
stops.date_confidence: attested that the device existed and that he performed with it in taverns and cafes (es.wikipedia); no date, workshop, or surviving example is recorded anywhere, so 1895 is a placeholder inside his cafe years and not a documented date.
stops.campa: He builds himself a device that holds a harmonica at his mouth while his hands stay on the guitar, so that one man on a cafe floor sounds like two. With it he works the taverns and cafes of the turn of the century, singing his own verses, a one-man orchestra in a city whose orchestras are trios of flute, violin, and guitar. No date and no workshop is recorded for the invention. The man who set type and drove a tram builds the thing the job requires and carries it to the job.
suggested_refs: Villoldo's harmonica-and-guitar apparatus, described but never depicted in the sources consulted

stops.name: Café de Hansen, Palermo: the tango the owner forbids
stops.date_confidence: attested that a Villoldo tango so excited Hansen's patrons that the owner forbade the musicians to play it (es.wikipedia, 'Café de Hansen'), and that the cafe operated 1877-1912. The year 1898 is a placeholder inside that span; the source gives no date for the incident. Coordinate corrected to the Sarmiento and Figueroa Alcorta site, where the Planetario now stands.
stops.campa: In the Palermo woods, where the Planetario now stands at Sarmiento and Figueroa Alcorta, Hansen's cafe serves well-off men who drive out from the centre for the night. It runs from 1877 until Anchorena has it pulled down in 1912, and the guardia vieja plays there. One night a tango of Villoldo's excites the customers so far that the owner forbids the musicians to play it again. The music is not respectable, and the carriages come out to Palermo at night for that reason and no other.
suggested_refs: The site of the Café de Hansen in the Palermo woods, demolished 1912 by order of Joaquín S. de Anchorena

stops.name: San Telmo, the cafes and the compadrito
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: San Telmo's cafes and dance academias are standard in the historiography of the guardia vieja, but no source names Villoldo at a San Telmo address. Date is a placeholder inside his cafe years; the stop records milieu, not a documented visit.
stops.campa: South of the Plaza, in the old city the fever emptied, the cafes and dance academias of San Telmo hold the other half of the circuit: payadores trading improvised decimas, milongueros, the compadrito with his knife and his slicked hair. No source puts Villoldo at a named San Telmo address. The milieu is documented and he is documented inside it, writing the compadrito as a character with a name and a neighbourhood rather than as a warning. Every room on this circuit is now pulled down or turned to other use. The character sung in them is still walking around.
suggested_refs: The cafes and academias de baile of San Telmo in the guardia vieja decades
sources: General tango historiography on San Telmo's role in early tango; no Villoldo-specific citation found

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the melody and the violinist Casimiro Alcorta
stops.date_confidence: open contradiction, deliberately unresolved. es.wikipedia's 'El choclo' dates the melody to about 1898 and reports that some sources credit it to Casimiro Alcorta rather than Villoldo, without settling the question; en.wikipedia's article on the same piece does not mention Alcorta at all. es.wikipedia's own Alcorta entry lists El choclo among his works but narrates no dispute. Tagged reconstruction throughout.
stops.campa: The tune that will be called El Choclo takes shape around this year. Some historians give it not to Villoldo but to Casimiro Alcorta, a Black violinist of the Buenos Aires dance floors who died poor in 1913 and is now nearly forgotten; the Spanish encyclopedia raises the claim without settling it, and the English one does not mention him. Alcorta's own entry lists El Choclo among his works and says nothing of a dispute. The melody is older than its title, and the question of whose hand first drew it is open.
suggested_refs: The disputed authorship of the El Choclo melody, and the biography of Casimiro Alcorta (died 1913)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the five pen names
stops.date_confidence: attested that he used the five pseudonyms (es. and en.wikipedia); no date attaches to any of them, so 1900 is a placeholder. The birth surname is printed inconsistently within es.wikipedia itself as Ghigiola and Ghigiolla, and no primary register was consulted.
stops.campa: He signs himself A. Gregorio, Fray Pimiento, Gregorio Gimenez, Angel Arroyo, and Mario Reguero, according to whether the page is a song sheet, a comic verse, or a column. The practice is ordinary for a popular writer working four trades at once, and it costs him later: one of the pen names, Arroyo, has been mistaken for a family surname and printed as his own. His birth registry gives Ghigiola, or Ghigiolla. The sources cannot agree on the spelling of the name he was born with.
suggested_refs: Song sheets and newspaper columns signed A. Gregorio, Fray Pimiento, Gregorio Giménez, Ángel Arroyo and Mario Reguero

stops.name: Restaurante El Americano, Cangallo 966: El Choclo premieres as a danza criolla
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by es. and en.wikipedia, in both the Villoldo article and the article on the piece, together with the address Cangallo 966, today Teniente General Perón 966. Coordinate corrected here to the OSM geocode of that address; an earlier pass carried a pin about 300 m northwest. The quoted couplet is verbatim at Letras.com but its assignment to the 1903 lyric layer is inference, since es.wikipedia describes that layer without printing it.
stops.campa: Tango is barred from respectable rooms, so Jose Luis Roncallo, who conducts a classical orchestra at the Restaurante El Americano on Cangallo, agrees to play his friend's new piece on one condition: that the programme call it a danza criolla. On the third of November the diners hear El Choclo without being told what it is. The title is street language for an ear of corn and for several things besides. Within two years it is on sale as sheet music; within fifty it is playing in Hollywood under another name.
stops.quote: De un grano nace la planta / que más tarde nos da el choclo
stops.quote_source: 'El Choclo,' opening lines of the Villoldo lyric as printed on Letras.com; assignment to the 1903 original layer rather than a later one is inference
suggested_refs: The building at Teniente General Perón 966, San Nicolás, formerly Cangallo 966, site of the Restaurante El Americano

stops.name: Buenos Aires, El Porteñito puts the compadrito in the first person
stops.date_confidence: contested by three years and resolved toward the dedicated source: es.wikipedia's article 'El porteñito' dates the premiere to 1903, while en.wikipedia's works list places it loosely circa 1900. The recording dates for Gobbi, Vivianne and Rodríguez de Gobbi come from the same es.wikipedia article. Month and day default to January 1.
stops.campa: He gives the city a self-portrait in the first person: a young man of Buenos Aires, quick with his feet and his knife, who dances the tango and answers to a nickname. The premiere is 1903, though loose works lists place it near 1900. He records it himself around its debut; Alfredo Gobbi cuts it for Victor in December 1907, Andree Vivianne for Odeon the same year, and Flora Rodriguez de Gobbi for the Gath y Chaves label in 1909 or 1910. The compadrito now has a song he sings about himself.
stops.quote: Soy hijo de Buenos Aires, por apodo 'El porteñito'
stops.quote_source: 'El Porteñito,' opening line, lyrics as printed on Letras.com, credited there to Ángel Villoldo
suggested_refs: Early discs of El Porteñito: Villoldo's own, Gobbi's RCA Victor side of 7 December 1907, Vivianne's Odeón of 1907

stops.name: Bar Reconquista, La Morocha written before dawn
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year, and to the circumstances by Enrique Saborido's own 1928 interview account as relayed by es.wikipedia: a wager among friends, the music written between about 5:00 and 6:30 a.m. at the Bar Reconquista, the dancer Lola Candales as inspiration. No street number for the bar was located, so the stop takes the canonical Buenos Aires pin. Month and day default to January 1.
stops.campa: A wager among friends at the Bar Reconquista: the Uruguayan Enrique Saborido is challenged to make a tango for the dancer Lola Candales, and by his own telling in 1928 he writes the music between five and half past six in the morning. Villoldo puts words in the woman's mouth, a dark-haired criolla who introduces herself and is proud of it. La Morocha is sung within days. Its printed score will travel to Paris in the luggage of rich young Argentines and in the kit of sailors who learned the step ashore.
stops.quote_source: 'La Morocha,' opening line, music Enrique Saborido and lyrics Ángel Villoldo, as printed on Letras.com
suggested_refs: Saborido's 1928 interview account of the night at the Bar Reconquista

stops.name: Buenos Aires, El Choclo goes on sale as sheet music
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by es.wikipedia's 'El choclo' for the sheet-music publication; the same article distinguishes four lyric layers, Villoldo's 1903 original, his own 'Cariño puro,' Marambio Catán's malevo version and Discépolo's of 1947, without printing the first. Month and day default to January 1.
stops.campa: El Choclo goes on sale as printed music two years after the night at El Americano. Villoldo writes more than one lyric for his own tune, an agricultural first version about the corn itself and a second called Cariño puro; other hands follow with theirs. The piece leaves him then, as an object anyone can buy and take home, and that is how a tango written for one restaurant orchestra gets into parlours in cities where nobody has heard of Buenos Aires. He keeps writing for the stage and the cafe.
suggested_refs: The 1905 printed edition of El Choclo, and the four successive lyric layers written for the same melody

stops.name: Camden, New Jersey: the first recording of La Morocha
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, the matrix number B 3.555-1, the performer Flora Rodríguez de Gobbi with Los Gobbi, and the country: es.wikipedia's 'La morocha (tango)' states the Victor session was made in the United States, correcting an earlier hedge that placed it in Buenos Aires or Paris. The city pin is a reconstruction: no studio is named by the source, and Camden is Victor's plant.
stops.campa: On the twenty-third of July the Victor company records La Morocha in the United States, matrix B 3.555-1, sung by Flora Rodriguez de Gobbi with the ensemble Los Gobbi. It is among the first tangos ever put on a disc, and the singer is a Chilean woman married to an Argentine bandleader, cutting an Uruguayan's melody and a porteno's words for a North American label. Villoldo is not in the room. The song is already travelling faster than the man who wrote it.
suggested_refs: Victor matrix B 3.555-1, 23 July 1906, Los Gobbi with Flora Rodríguez de Gobbi

stops.name: Paris, the first tango scores reach Europe
stops.date_confidence: attested that La Morocha was among the first tango scores to reach Europe, carried by young Argentines of wealthy families and by sailors (es.wikipedia). The sales figure is contested: en.wikipedia gives more than 280,000 sheet-music copies, es.wikipedia's 'Enrique Saborido' about 100,000. The pin is the corpus's generic Paris coordinate, flagged in prior journeys as too imprecise; it marks the city only, no address being attested.
stops.campa: The printed score of La Morocha reaches Europe among the first tango music to do so, carried by young Argentines of wealthy families going over for the season and by sailors who learned the dance in the port. Paris takes up the step before it takes the music seriously; the tango becomes a fashion in rooms where nobody knows the name of the man who wrote the words. Sales of the sheet run to about a hundred thousand copies by one account and more than two hundred and eighty thousand by another.
suggested_refs: The first tango scores circulating in Paris, carried from Buenos Aires by travellers and sailors

stops.name: Paris, the Gath y Chaves recordings with the Gobbis
stops.date_confidence: contradiction between encyclopedias, one branch untenable. es.wikipedia dates the Gath y Chaves-sponsored trip to 1903, en.wikipedia to 1907; 1903 cannot stand, because es.wikipedia's own 'Alfredo Eusebio Gobbi' has Gobbi and Flora Rodríguez marrying in 1905 and its 'El porteñito' dates her Gath y Chaves recordings to 1909-1910. 1907 is used and the conflict is recorded. No Paris studio, label partner, or address is named anywhere; the pin marks the city only.
stops.campa: The department store Gath y Chaves pays for three musicians to cross the Atlantic and record: Alfredo Gobbi, Flora Rodriguez, and Villoldo. In Paris he cuts sides for several companies and plays the tango for people who have only danced it. He is forty-six, a cafe singer out of Barracas, and the capital of Europe is learning a music his own city still keeps out of its good rooms. What he does not do is stay. He goes home to the same circuit of theatres and taverns he left.
suggested_refs: The Gath y Chaves department store's sponsorship of the Paris tango recordings, and the label's Buenos Aires catalogue

stops.name: Paris, the society of authors and composers
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to date: es.wikipedia attests the affiliation with France's society of authors and composers to collect royalties but gives no year, and no registration record was reached. The date placed here follows the 1907 trip and is not sourced. Pin is the generic Paris coordinate, no address being attested.
stops.campa: He joins the French society of authors and composers so that the money his tunes earn in Europe reaches him in Buenos Aires. It is an unglamorous act and a shrewd one: El Choclo and La Morocha are being played in rooms he will never enter, and a popular composer with no publisher behind him collects by registering or does not collect at all. No date survives for the affiliation. The songs are earning money in France while he goes on working the taverns of Buenos Aires.
suggested_refs: French authors' society registration records for Villoldo, not reached in this research pass

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Odeón session with the Rondalla Vázquez
stops.date_confidence: weakly sourced and flagged as such: the session comes from a single prior research summary naming Odeón Records and the Rondalla Vázquez, and could not be corroborated against any discography or label ledger, none of which were reached. Retained as a thread, not a fact. Month and day default to January 1.
stops.campa: A recording session in Buenos Aires for Odeon with the Rondalla Vazquez is reported for this year. The report comes from a single summary that could not be matched against a discography, so it stands here as a weak thread rather than a fact. The industry it belongs to is real enough: within a decade of El Choclo the city has record shops, catalogues, and a public that buys tangos by the title, and Villoldo's name is on the labels of a music that was unprintable when he began.
suggested_refs: Odeón Records' Buenos Aires catalogue of 1907, not reached in this research pass
sources: Single prior research summary citing Odeón Records and the Rondalla Vázquez; not independently corroborated

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Los mamertos in the centenary year
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year: a comic parody recorded in the voice of a drunk character (en.wikipedia; es.wikipedia, 'La morocha (tango)'). No label, matrix, or date within the year is given by either source. Month and day default to January 1.
stops.campa: In the centenary year of the May Revolution he records Los mamertos, a comic number performed in the voice of a drunk. He is fifty, and the range has not changed since the circus ring: the borracho, the compadrito, the swindler, each given a voice and let loose for three minutes. Buenos Aires spends 1910 celebrating itself in marble and electric light, and the man who wrote its dance music spends it playing a drunk into a recording horn. The tango is an industry around him without making him rich.
suggested_refs: The 1910 recording of Los mamertos, no copy of which was located in this research pass

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the lament for Aparicio Saravia
stops.date_confidence: the opening line is verbatim at Letras.com, but that page carries no songwriter credit at all, unlike the other Villoldo entries, so the piece is his only by sitting in his artist index. The dating is inference: Aparicio Saravia was killed in the 1904 Uruguayan rising, so the lament cannot be earlier; no composition year was found.
stops.campa: Aparicio Saravia, the Uruguayan caudillo, is shot in the 1904 rising across the river and dies of the wound; Villoldo writes him a lament. The piece is undated, and the page that carries it shows no author credit at all, only its place in his catalogue. What the dating rests on is the death: the song cannot be older than the man it mourns. The porteno comic writer turns, once, to the payador's elegy, and opens it with a flat statement of his own grief.
stops.quote_source: 'Homenaje a Saravia,' opening line, lyrics as printed on Letras.com; the page shows no authorship credit and the piece sits in Villoldo's artist index
suggested_refs: The Letras.com text of Homenaje a Saravia, uncredited on its own page

stops.name: Buenos Aires, songs for the Podestá stage
stops.date_confidence: attested that he collaborated with the Podestá family, including José María 'Pepe' Podestá and Pablo Podestá, and with the actress Angelina Pagano, supplying comic songs and musical numbers (en.wikipedia). No theatre, production title, or date survives in any source reached; the year is a placeholder.
stops.campa: He supplies songs and musical numbers to the Podesta family, the circus dynasty who turned the criollo drama into Argentine theatre, and to the actress Angelina Pagano. No theatre, no date, no title of a production survives for the collaboration. The stage is where his verses were meant to land: sung by a character in costume, to an audience that came for the sainete and the pantomime. The tango reaches the middle classes through the theatre door long before it reaches them through the ballroom.
stops.quote_source: 'Testamento de Un Paisano,' opening line, lyrics as printed on Letras.com, credited there to Ángel Villoldo
suggested_refs: The Podestá family's theatrical repertory and Angelina Pagano's companies, in which no Villoldo production has been identified

stops.name: Buenos Aires, El Cachafaz dressed better than his means
stops.date_confidence: the lyric text is verbatim at Letras.com, whose credit reads Angel Villoldo and Manuel Aróztegui, Aróztegui as composer, so Villoldo is the lyricist and not sole author. No date is given for the piece anywhere reached, and 1908 is a placeholder; an earlier pass quoted only the first five words of the line and called them the whole opening line.
stops.campa: With music by Manuel Aroztegui he writes the cachafaz, the flash gentleman of the barrio, a type dressed better than his means and known by everyone on the block. Villoldo's people are named, local, and seen from the street the way a neighbour sees them. He neither moralises about the compadrito nor romanticises him. He describes the clothes, lets the man talk, and leaves the audience to laugh or not laugh as it pleases. The song does not tell anyone what to think of him.
stops.quote: El cachafaz es un tipo de vestir muy elegante
stops.quote_source: 'El Cachafaz,' full opening line, lyrics as printed on Letras.com; page credit reads Angel Villoldo and Manuel Aróztegui
suggested_refs: The Letras.com text of El Cachafaz, credited to Villoldo with music by Manuel Aróztegui

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Matufias, or the art of living
stops.date_confidence: the opening line is verbatim at Letras.com, credited there to Villoldo. No composition or publication date was found for the piece in any source reached; the date here is a placeholder inside the centenary years and carries no evidentiary weight.
stops.campa: Under the title Matufias, or the art of living, he writes the swindle as the century's governing principle: the fixed contract, the padded account, the man who prospers by arrangement. It is the Buenos Aires of the centenary boom, of grain money and land speculation and municipal favour, and the songwriter of the cafes is reporting on it in rhyme. He had been a journalist. The habit does not leave him when he changes trades; it only changes metre.
stops.quote: Es el siglo en que vivimos
stops.quote_source: 'Matufias (O el arte de vivir),' opening line, lyrics as printed on Letras.com, credited there to Ángel Villoldo
suggested_refs: The Letras.com text of Matufias (o el arte de vivir)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the ordinance and the fifty-peso fine
stops.date_confidence: the opening line is verbatim at Letras.com, credited there to Villoldo, and names a municipal ordinance on morals. No ordinance has been identified and no date for the song was found; the year here is a placeholder and the identification of the specific ordinance is not made.
stops.campa: A municipal ordinance on public morals arrives with a fifty-peso fine attached, and Villoldo answers it with a song warning the city to watch out. The authorities that legislate against improper dancing and improper language are the same ones that will not let his tango be called a tango inside a restaurant. He does not petition them. He writes a comic number about the fine and sells it around the taverns, which is the argument a tavern singer has to hand.
stops.quote_source: 'Cuidado Con Los 50,' opening line, lyrics as printed on Letras.com, credited there to Ángel Villoldo
suggested_refs: The Buenos Aires municipal morals ordinance answered by 'Cuidado con los 50,' not identified in this research pass

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the centenary songbook
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by en.wikipedia, which names a collection of Argentine popular songs published in 1916 and ties it to the centenary of the Declaration of Independence. No publisher or copy was located. Month and day default to January 1.
stops.campa: For the centenary of the declaration of independence at Tucuman he contributes to a collection of Argentine popular songs. The man whose music was billed as a danza criolla to get it past a restaurant manager is now inside the official commemoration of the nation. He is fifty-five. Thirteen years separate the restaurant manager who would not let the word tango be printed on a programme from the committee that puts his music in the nation's centenary book, and he lives through both.
suggested_refs: The 1916 collection of Argentine popular songs published for the independence centenary

stops.name: The German front, the band without the anthem
stops.date_confidence: single-witness anecdote, tagged reconstruction. es.wikipedia sources it solely to the journalist Tito Livio Foppa, who recounts a 1916 banquet for the foreign press held 'en el frente alemán' at which a band lacking the score of the Argentine anthem played El Choclo instead. No corroboration exists and no site is named; the pin is a German centroid marking the country only. An earlier pass tagged this attested and pinned it in Buenos Aires, contradicting the claim itself.
stops.campa: The journalist Tito Livio Foppa tells a story: at a banquet for the foreign press on the German front in wartime, a military band is asked to greet the Argentine guests with their national anthem, has no score for it, and plays El Choclo instead. Nobody corroborates him and the site is never named. Whether it happened or not, the story can only be told at all because the tune is loose enough in the world by 1916 that a European bandmaster knows it from memory and hears a country in it.
suggested_refs: Tito Livio Foppa's account of the 1916 wartime press banquet, the sole witness to the anecdote
sources: Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Ángel Villoldo', citing Tito Livio Foppa

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Gardel and Razzano record Cantar eterno
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by en.wikipedia. The recording location is presumed Buenos Aires and is not stated by the source; month and day default to January 1. No meeting, correspondence, or photograph connects Villoldo and Gardel personally, so the relation documented is one-directional and musical only.
stops.campa: Carlos Gardel and Jose Razzano put Cantar eterno on a record, two years before Villoldo dies. Gardel is the voice that will carry the tango out of the cafe and into the century, and the material he is singing here is the older man's. The transmission runs one way and it runs quietly: no meeting is recorded, no photograph, no letter. A song written by the man who invented the trade is taken up by the man who will become its face. That is the whole of the documented contact between them.
suggested_refs: The 1917 Gardel-Razzano recording of Cantar eterno

stops.name: Buenos Aires, death at fifty-eight
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day and the age by es. and en.wikipedia. No source names the street, house, hospital, or cause of death, and none consulted documents a wife or a child; that absence is a gap in the record and not a finding of bachelorhood. Pin is the canonical Buenos Aires coordinate, no address being attested.
stops.campa: He dies in Buenos Aires at fifty-eight. No source names the street, the house, or the illness, and no source consulted records a wife or a child. Sixteen years have passed since the night at El Americano. In that time the music he wrote for a restaurant orchestra to disguise has been recorded in three countries, sold as sheet music by the hundred thousand, and set into the official songbook of the republic's centenary. He leaves the tunes and no address.
